title: Seething Lane by Jack Jewers - Book review
transcript: >> Hello and welcome to theater reviews with Paul Seven. If you watch me regularly, I know you you won't expect me to be reviewing a novel. Um, but I think you'll be interested in this one because a substantial part of Jack Jewers' gripping whodunit, Seething Lane, is set in a theater at the time of the restoration of the monarchy. The book is the second in what deserves to become a long-running series of mystery novels featuring the famous diarist Samuel Pepys as a proto-detective. In this mixture of fact and fiction, Sam, who was a fan of theater, fact, spends time at the Theatre Royal in Drury Lane investigating some murders. Fiction. Now, for anyone interested in theater, the preparations for a production of As You Like It provide many fascinating insights into what went on backstage in the latter part of the 17th century. Women had only just been allowed to appear on stage, and Nell Gwyn was wowing the crowds as well as King Charles II. Sam, Nell, and the King aren't the only real people in this book, and if you know your theatrical history, well, you won't be surprised at one of the revelations of Sam's investigation. Mr. Jewers' historical knowledge also covers London post-Great Fire and the feverish politics of the time. He wears his research lightly, but it does help enormously in his evocation of life in London. The muddy streets, the primitive system of law and order, the transport. Did you know you could hire a horse like you might hire a car? And especially the bitter cold weather of the winter of 1670. Samuel Pepys and his right-hand man Will Hewer recruited by the king to look into the grisly murders of someone close to his son and of a mysterious second person. The son in question is illegitimate but controversially tipped to be his successor. This investigation comes on top of Sam also being required to spy on a firebrand preacher. I suppose inevitably the two activities turn out to be linked um although I found the connection slightly stretched credibility but no matter there's plenty of intrigue and excitement and more unpleasant deaths as the detective team peel back the layers of a conspiracy and find themselves in danger. Now the book is a pastiche of Samuel Pepys way of writing a diary but Mr. Jewers writes in a tight easy-to-read style while it suggests the language of the period is never obscure or anachronistic and always thrilling. Seething incidentally is where Sam lives and works and where the first murders take place. If you're familiar with the real Samuel Pepys well you may be surprised to find the corrupt official who enjoyed sexual liaisons with servants and actresses has been transformed into a moral beacon who is devoted to his wife. But this is fiction. Mr. Jewers Samuel Pepys is determined despite obstacles and threats to uncover the truth and in doing so he becomes a hero we admire and care about whose adventures keep us turning those pages. >> >> If you found this review interesting, please like and comment.
